about: The SQL Server source half of the silent-differences catalogue (ADR 0019): how each SQL Server construct behaves, in vocabulary terms. Its entries are Annex C's, keyed by entry ID, and the engine's tests check every cell against docs/spec/annex-c-differences-sql-server.md and every name in 'operations', 'types' and 'arguments' against the operation vocabulary. 'arguments' holds names in the Vocabulary cell that are arguments of an operation (the POWER of numeric_function), not vocabulary entries. 'wording' is the report's plain wording of SQL Server's behaviour, for caveats and manual-work reasons; an entry has it once the report needs it. The version is the hash of 'entries'.

entries.section: 3. Numbers: division, implicit conversion, decimal precision
entries.behaviour: The order in which rows are added is not defined, and a parallel plan can change it from one run to the next. Floating-point addition is not associative, so the last digits can differ
entries.evidence: Inferred. Added by the owner in [How does reconciliation generate data and compare results?](https://github.com/Bach-To-The-Future/data-migration/issues/13)

entries.section: 3. Numbers: division, implicit conversion, decimal precision
entries.example: `SUM(c)` or `AVG(c)` over an `int` column holding 2147483647, 1 and -5
entries.behaviour: Arithmetic overflow error 8115, although the final total, 2147483643, fits in `int`: the running total is kept in `int` and fails as soon as it leaves the range. The order in which rows are added is not defined and a plan (parallel or not) can change it, so whether the same rows fail can depend on the plan's aggregation order
entries.evidence: SQL Server half tested on the 2022 CU27 sandbox for the order shown; the dependence on plan order and the Spark half are inferred. Added by the owner in [Engine skeleton: one view converted end to end as a preview run](https://github.com/Bach-To-The-Future/data-migration/issues/36)
entries.wording: SQL Server raises an overflow error when a running total leaves int, even if the final total fits, and whether it does can depend on the plan's aggregation order

entries.example: `id int IDENTITY(1, 1)` and code that assumes dense values
entries.behaviour: Each value is generated from the current seed and increment, on any integer type. Consecutive values are not guaranteed: concurrent inserts, failed or rolled-back statements and restarts leave gaps ([IDENTITY][m-identity])
The last identity value generated in the scope, session or table ([SCOPE_IDENTITY][m-scopeidentity], [@@IDENTITY][m-atidentity])

entries.example: `SELECT * INTO new_table FROM t` where `t` has an identity column
entries.behaviour: The new column inherits the `IDENTITY` property ([SELECT INTO][m-selectinto])

entries.example: `BEGIN TRAN; INSERT a …; INSERT b …; ROLLBACK`
entries.behaviour: Every statement in the transaction is undone ([transaction guide][m-txguide])

entries.example: Three inserts, the second violating a constraint, `XACT_ABORT OFF`, no `TRY`
entries.behaviour: Only the failing statement is rolled back; the batch continues and the third insert runs ([XACT_ABORT][m-xactabort], [transaction guide][m-txguide])
The whole transaction is rolled back and the batch ends ([XACT_ABORT][m-xactabort])

entries.example: An explicit transaction with `XACT_ABORT OFF` where one statement fails and the code then commits
entries.behaviour: The failing statement is rolled back and the transaction can continue and commit the rest ([XACT_ABORT][m-xactabort])

entries.example: `INSERT` of a duplicate key into a table with a primary key or unique constraint, often inside `TRY…CATCH` as an upsert
entries.behaviour: The insert fails and the error is caught ([TRY...CATCH][m-trycatch])

entries.example: `BEGIN TRY … END TRY BEGIN CATCH … END CATCH`
entries.behaviour: Catches errors of severity above 10 that do not close the connection. Does not catch warnings, or compile errors at the same execution level ([TRY...CATCH][m-trycatch])

entries.example: `MERGE … ON t.code = s.code` with string keys
entries.behaviour: Keys match ignoring case and trailing spaces (rows 2.1, 2.4), so the row is updated

entries.example: `UPDATE t SET … FROM t JOIN s …` where several `s` rows match one `t` row
entries.behaviour: No error; which source row is used is undefined ([UPDATE][m-update])
Returns one row for every row inserted, updated or deleted ([MERGE][m-merge], [OUTPUT][m-output])
`AFTER` and `INSTEAD OF` triggers fire for each action ([MERGE][m-merge])

entries.example: `MERGE` with one unconditional `WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE` and several source rows per target row
entries.behaviour: `MERGE` cannot update the same row more than once, or update and delete the same row; the page does not state the delete-only case ([MERGE][m-merge])
